lines.text: Indoor hobbies offer relaxation, creativity, and personal fulfilment, and each comes with its own rich vocabulary. Reading remains one of the most popular pastimes — browsing bookshops, joining book clubs, and building personal libraries. Cooking and baking have become creative outlets: people experiment with recipes, master techniques like kneading, whisking, and folding, and share their results on social media. Crafts encompass knitting (using needles and yarn), crocheting (using a hook and yarn), sewing (with needle and thread or a sewing machine), embroidery (decorative stitching), and cross-stitch. Model building involves assembling miniature replicas of vehicles, buildings, or figures using kits with detailed instructions. Board gaming has experienced a renaissance, with hobbyists collecting complex strategy games and hosting regular game nights. Indoor gardening — cultivating houseplants, terrariums, and herb gardens on windowsills — has boomed in popularity. Puzzling includes jigsaw puzzles, crosswords, Sudoku, and logic puzzles. Calligraphy (beautiful handwriting) and bullet journaling (creative planning notebooks) combine art with organisation. Collecting — stamps, coins, vinyl records, vintage items — is a hobby with its own communities and terminology. Music practice, whether learning guitar, piano, or joining a choir, provides both creative expression and social connection. These hobbies provide not just entertainment but vocabulary-rich contexts for natural English conversation.

lines.text: Knitting has had a massive revival in Britain, especially among younger adults. Yarn shops, 'stitch and natter' groups (knit and chat), and online communities like Ravelry have made it trendy. The vocabulary — 'cast on', 'purl', 'cable stitch' — is entering broader conversation.
